title: Seneca's three questions
hook: each night his teacher Sextius asked: what fault did I cure today, what failing did I resist, in what am I better? (Seneca, On Anger 3.36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the morning preview, with Marcus at dawn. Your line was I'll meet them kindly. Did someone difficult show up right on schedule, and did you see them coming? Day one hundred five.

Yesterday was the morning. Today, the other end of the day: the minutes after the lamp goes out. In Rome, long ago, a man lies in the dark. His wife has gone quiet, because she knows his habit. And instead of scrolling through the day's worries, he goes through the day itself, deed by deed and word by word, like an accountant going through a ledger. The man is Seneca, a writer, statesman and Stoic. He learned the habit from an older teacher, and he wrote it down in a book about anger. Today: Seneca's three questions.
screen: `AFTER THE LAMP GOES OUT.` → `HIS WIFE KNOWS HIS HABIT.` → `THE DAY, LIKE A LEDGER.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Quintus Sextius, a Roman philosopher Seneca admired. Seneca says that at the end of each day, when Sextius went to bed, he would ask his own mind three questions. What bad habit of yours did you cure today? What failing did you stand up against? In what way are you better? That's a paraphrase; Seneca's Latin is short and sharp. And he adds the point of it all: anger, and every other fault, gets weaker when it knows it will be brought before a judge every evening. The judge here isn't a god or a priest. It's you. Look closely at the questions, because they aren't the ones we usually ask at night. The questions that usually turn up at night run differently: what went wrong, who wronged me, what did I forget? Those are questions about the world. Sextius's questions are about the self, and they're about repair. What did I mend? Where did I hold the line? Where did I grow? You can't answer them without looking honestly at your faults. But the frame points forward. It assumes you are someone who can change, and asks for the evidence. Seneca calls this kind of sleep especially good: calm, deep and free, after the mind has been praised or warned. On an ordinary Tuesday, it might sound like this: today I didn't snap when the train was late. Today I finally sent the apology. Today I was a little more patient than last Tuesday. Small repairs, noticed.
screen: `SEXTIUS, AT BEDTIME.` · `CURED, RESISTED, BETTER.` · `A JUDGE EVERY EVENING.` · `QUESTIONS ABOUT REPAIR.` · then, large: `WHAT DID I MEND?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask the three questions tonight. For now, a rehearsal. Settle, and breathe. Think back over yesterday, or this day so far. First question: what habit did I work on? Second: what did I resist, even once? Third: in what way am I a little better? If an answer comes, let it be small and true. If nothing comes, that's an answer too; just notice it without a verdict. Then let the day go and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Seneca's three questions. What did I cure, what did I resist, in what am I better: asked each night, from his teacher Sextius. Today's word.
Your line: what did I mend. Tonight, lights out, before your phone gets the last word, ask the three questions and find one small repair. Day one hundred five.

howItsDone: Some people who follow Stoic practice end the day with an evening review drawn from Seneca's On Anger 3.36, going over the day and asking what they improved, what they resisted, and how they grew.

original.note: Latin: every day, daily. Seneca says the mind should be called to account every day.

trapdoor: what you thought: lying in bed replaying everything that went wrong.
what it means: three questions about repair, asked each night: what did I cure, what did I resist, in what am I better.
what a scholar hears: Quintus Sextius founded a short-lived Roman school that mixed Stoic and Pythagorean ideas, and the nightly self-review echoes the Pythagoreans.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: removed "two thousand years ago" and "the generation before, who ran his own small school" (not in De Ira 3.36); "hour by hour" changed to "deed by deed and word by word", closer to Seneca's text; the listener is no longer told what they ask at night; cotidie pronunciation corrected to koh-TEE-dee-ay (long i in cotīdiē).
Seneca's De Ira 3.36 is paraphrased throughout (the three questions; faults weaken before a daily judge; his wife falling silent; the sleep that follows). Confirm each paraphrase against the Latin.
Quintus Sextius: 'a Roman philosopher of the generation before, who ran his own small school' mixing Stoic and Pythagorean ideas (trapdoor): confirm.
Latin cotidie and the paraphrase that the mind should be called to account daily: confirm.
